THE SOTERIOLOGY OF RECOGNITION: THE JĪVANMUKTA AND THE TRANSMISSION

Why liberation is recognition, how the IPVV proves it, and the guru-paramparā — the closing sum (V3N–P)

  • 026-08-11. The recognition-thesis is not only epistemology and metaphysics; it is a soteriology. The
  • VV closes on the liberation: since liberation is from the recognition alone, the elaborate
  • fort-yogas are useless; the recognition is the clear, effort-less means; and its fruit is the
  • vanmukta — the one liberated while still living. This essay expounds the soteriology: why liberation
  • recognition (not effort), how the IPVV argues it, the bond and the liberation, and the transmission
  • he guru-paramparā). It is the soteriology essay, unique to the completed IPVV — the region neither the
  • K nor Ratié develops.*

1. Why liberation is recognition

  • e soteriological claim of the IPVV is precise and radical:
"Since liberation is from the recognition alone, all the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here;
this is the clear means, effort-less, un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit." (V3P)
  • The argument.* Liberation is from the recognition *alone. Why? Because — as the whole system has
  • tablished — the self was never absent; it is only mis-positioned. The bondage is the misreading (the
  • entification of the self as a thing among things); the liberation is the removal of that misreading.
  • d the removal of a misreading is not an achievement; it is a recognition — the re-cognition of what
  • s always there.
  • The contrast with effort.** The breath-controls and the effort-yogas are "artificial"; "the un-made
  • ality does not yield to a sixteenth part of such effort." If the self was never absent, no effort can
  • d it; and if the bondage is a misreading, no effort can remove it by adding something. Only the
  • cognition — the turning that sees what was always present — can do it. The recognition is "the clear
  • ans, effort-less, un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit."
  • The lover-image (the mechanism).** The lover stands near; as long as he is not recognized, he cannot
  • enjoyed. The world-Lord is always present, always near; he is not experienced in his own splendor
  • til the recognition arises. The recognition turns the un-known nearness into the joy of union. This
  • the soteriological mechanism: nothing is added (the lover was near); the recognition turns the near
  • to the enjoyed.

2. The bond: the paśu's un-common creation (V3O)

  • e soteriology requires an account of the bondage. The IPVV gives it in the tattvasaṅgraha (V3O):
  • The bound one creates, after his own fashion — but his creation is un-common.** It is private,
  • r-knower, per-moment, vanishing with him. And it does not stand on its own; it is *sustained by the
  • rd's creation*.
"The whole difference of bound and liberated hangs on a single fact: the bound one does not know
his own power. He forgets that the world he builds is built with the Lord's own materials." (V3O)
  • The construction-action is the bond.** "By it the māyā-power binds the animal." Even the seemingly
  • ee constructions — "I, the king, stand," "I have slain my enemy" — are, on inspection,
  • her-dependent; the bound one's freedom is only apparent, resting on the Lord's.
  • The threefold māyā.** The māyā works in three ways: the appearance of the void, the appearance of the
  • posite, the mere negation — spreading through the three stains (āṇava, māyīya, kārma).

3. The liberation: the abandonment of construction (V3O)

  • ainst the bound one's un-common creation stands the Lord's common creation — clear-manifestation,
  • ver constructed, always whole. And there is a path out of the prison:
"When, by the thinning of the constructions and the gathering of the mind to one point, the bound one
comes to the 'I-this' of the Lord, his animal-ness is destroyed and the Lord-ness shines." (V3O)
  • The mechanism of the liberation.** The liberation is the abandonment of construction — the thinning of
  • e vikalpas, the gathering of the mind to one point, the coming to the "I-this" of the Lord. This is
  • t an addition of something new; it is the removal of the constructions (the misreadings) that hid the
  • rd. The liberation is the recognition, because it is the removal of the false construction, not the
  • tainment of a new state.

4. The jīvanmukta (V3P)

  • e fruit of the recognition is the jīvanmukta — the one liberated while still living:
"The one who, even in the body, is already free, and who at the fall of the body is simply the
supreme Lord. This, Abhinavagupta says, is the most wondrous thing of all — liberation in this very
life." (V3P)
  • The claim.** Liberation is not the destruction of the body or the escape from the world; it is the
  • cognition that liberates while still living. The jīvanmukta lives in the body, deals with the world,
  • t is already free — because the false identification has been removed, not the body.
  • The significance for the recognition-thesis.** The jīvanmukta is the living proof that the
  • cognition-thesis is true: if liberation were an attainment (something added), it would require a new
  • ate; but it is a recognition (nothing added), so it can occur while the body and world remain. The
  • vanmukta is the recognition, lived. This is why "the most wondrous thing of all" is liberation in
  • is very life: because it is the removal of a misreading, not the acquisition of a state.

5. The transmission: the guru-paramparā (V3P)

  • e IPVV closes on the transmission of the teaching:
"Part of the teaching comes from the self (svataḥ); part from the śāstra (śāstrataḥ); and part must
come from the guru (gurutaḥ). For even the vision of the śāstra must be carried to its proper power
by the lineage of teachers." (V3P)
  • d Abhinava is stern:
"The book-studied knowledges, without the guru-order, practicing and teaching, ripen long in hell."
(V3P)
  • The line.** The transmission runs from the ādi-Śrīkaṇṭhanātha down through Durvāsa and Tryambakāditya,
  • e mental sons who carry the un-precedented, effort-less word.
  • Why the guru is necessary.** The teaching must be received from the living line, because the
  • cognition is not a proposition to be believed but an event to be triggered. The guru does not give a
  • w content; he points — he occasions the recognition of what was always there. This is why the
  • ok-studied knowledge without the guru-order is sterile: it is the content without the pointing, and
  • e recognition is not the content but the turning.

6. The soteriological argument, complete

  • e soteriology of recognition, completely stated:
  • The self was never absent (V1D) — so liberation cannot be an attainment.
  • The bondage is the misreading (the identification with the finite self-positioning) — so
  • beration cannot be an addition.
  • The liberation is the removal of the misreading — the recognition, the abandonment of
  • nstruction (V3O).
  • Therefore liberation is from the recognition alone (V3P) — the effort-less, clear means.
  • The fruit is the jīvanmukta — liberation in this very life, because it is a removal, not a state.
  • The recognition is transmitted by the guru-paramparā, because it is a pointing, not a
  • oposition (V3P).
  • The conclusion.** The soteriology completes the recognition-thesis. The epistemology said knowledge
  • the felt self-awareness; the metaphysics said action is the same self-awareness as the will; the
  • teriology says liberation is the same self-awareness recognized — the jīvanmukta, the one who, even in
  • e body, is free. Recognition is not only how we know and act; it is how we are liberated.

7. The boundary

  • e soteriology is [T] in the IPVV (the recognition-path, the jīvanmukta, the guru-paramparā) and it
  • llows from the first principles of the system. The one commitment is the same as everywhere: the
  • iversalization — the step from "each self re-cognizes itself" to "all selves are one Lord." The
  • vanmukta is the recognition of the per-field self as the Lord; the identity of all such Lords is the
  • ger. The soteriology is argued for the finite field; the one Lord is the commitment.

8. The significance

  • e soteriology is the completion of the recognition-thesis, and it is unique to the completed IPVV —
  • e region neither the IPK nor Ratié's book develops. It shows:
  • Why recognition is the path — because liberation is the removal of a misreading, not the
  • tainment of a state.
  • How the liberation works — the abandonment of construction, the coming to the "I-this" of the
  • rd.
  • What it produces — the jīvanmukta, the one liberated while living.
  • How it is transmitted — the guru-paramparā, the pointing that occasions the recognition.
  • e IPVV does not stop at the epistemology; it builds the path and closes on the jīvanmukta. This is
  • e soteriology of recognition — the final region of the system, and the completion of the recognition-
  • esis.
  • his is the soteriology essay. Liberation is from the recognition alone (V3P): because the self was
  • ver absent and the bondage is the misreading, the liberation is the removal of the misreading — the
  • cognition, the abandonment of construction (V3O). The fruit is the jīvanmukta, the one liberated while
  • ving (V3P); the transmission is the guru-paramparā, the pointing that occasions the recognition. This
  • mpletes the recognition-thesis as a soteriology. The universalization is the commitment.*
